english: Oh, I see / Ah, got it — a soft reaction when you just learned or understood something new.
usage: with 아 as a natural lead-in breath
past form, reacting to a past event they told you
examples: 아, 그렇구나.
Oh, I see.
the bare two-word reaction — just absorbing a new fact
A: 나 사실 부산 출신이야 / B: 아, 그렇구나. 어쩐지 사투리가.
A: I'm actually from Busan / B: Oh, I see. No wonder the accent.
everyday: pairs naturally with 어쩐지 when a clue clicks
A: 그 가게 월요일에 쉬어요 / B: 그렇군요. 알려주셔서 감사해요.
A: That shop is closed on Mondays / B: I see. Thanks for letting me know.
real situation: the polite 그렇군요 to a stranger who helped you
nuance: 그렇구나 (casual) / 그렇군요 (polite) is the 'oh, I see — that's news to me' you breathe out the instant a new fact clicks. It is built from 그렇다 'to be so' + the discovery ending -구나/-군요, which Korean reserves for something you have JUST taken in, so it always carries a faint flavor of fresh realization. The line to draw is against 그러게(요): 그렇구나 receives NEW information ('I didn't know that'), while 그러게 means 'right, I feel the same' about something you already shared — answer a surprising fact with 그러게요 and you sound like you knew all along. Reacting to a past event, shift to 그랬구나 'oh, so that happened.' The English-speaker pitfall is register: 'I see' feels neutral in English, so learners drop plain 그렇구나 on a boss or elder, but the bare -구나 is banmal; with anyone you keep -요 with, it must be 그렇군요, and to a senior even 그러시군요.

Answering surprising NEW info with 그러게요 instead of 그렇군요 — 그러게(요) means 'right, same here' about a shared feeling, so it implies you already knew; for genuinely new facts use 그렇구나/그렇군요.
Using present 그렇구나 for something that already happened — if a friend tells you about a past event, the natural reaction is the past form 그랬구나, not 그렇구나.

english: True / fair enough / come to think of it — used when you suddenly admit the other person has a point.
usage: conceding a point after a beat
realizing they have a point just now
examples: 하긴, 그건 그래.
Fair enough, that part's true.
the bare concession — granting one point
A: 지금 가도 차 막혀서 똑같아 / B: 하긴, 그냥 천천히 가자.
A: Even if we leave now traffic's the same / B: Fair enough, let's just go slow.
everyday: conceding and changing plans with a friend
A: 비 오는데 배달이 낫지 않아? / B: 하긴 그러네, 그냥 시키자.
A: It's raining, isn't delivery better? / B: Huh, you're right, let's just order.
real situation: 하긴 그러네 marks the exact moment you switch your mind
nuance: 하긴 is a casual discourse opener that means 'now that you put it that way, you've got a point' — a small step back where you reconsider and half-concede. It is the frozen, idiomatic shortening of 하기는 (하다 'to do' + the topic-contrast -기는), and it almost always opens the reply, usually as 하긴 그래 or 하긴 그러네. The contrast to keep clear is with 그러게(요): 그러게 means 'right, I already felt the same,' but 하긴 means 'I hadn't thought of it that way — but yes, fair.' That reconsideration nuance is the whole point. Register-wise it is firmly banmal-flavored, everywhere among friends and 20-30s coworkers off the clock, but in formal or business speech it sounds too offhand; there you say 그건 그렇네요 or 맞는 말씀이에요. The English-speaker pitfall is treating it as a full 'yes': 하긴 is a mild 'fair point,' not a strong agreement, and dropping it into a meeting reads as flippant.

Spelling or saying it as the full 하기는 in conversation — as a reaction it is the frozen short form 하긴; 하기는 in speech sounds stiff and unnatural.

english: No wonder / that explains it — said when new info finally explains something you found odd.
usage: reacting the moment an explanation lands
you'd already sensed something was up
that's why it seemed that way
examples: 어쩐지.
No wonder.
the bare one-word reaction when it all suddenly fits
A: 나 어제 밤새웠어 / B: 어쩐지 피곤해 보이더라.
A: I pulled an all-nighter / B: No wonder you looked tired.
everyday: 어쩐지 + -더라 ties the explanation to what you'd observed
A: 그 사람 사실 사장님 아들이래 / B: 어쩐지. 다들 조심하더라.
A: He's actually the boss's son / B: No wonder. Everyone was careful around him.
real situation: a long-standing puzzle finally clicks
nuance: 어쩐지 is the 'no wonder / that explains it' you say the moment a small mystery gets solved — you had quietly noticed something off, and the new fact snaps it into place. It is rooted in 어찌 'how/why' + the indefinite -ㄴ지, so under the hood it carries 'so THAT'S why,' and it loves to pair with the retrospective ending -더라 (어쩐지 …하더라) to replay what you had observed. The dangerous look-alike is 어쨌든 'anyway/regardless': they share the 어쩌- stem and beginners blur them, but 어쩐지 is causal ('that's the reason') while 어쨌든 dismisses the reason ('regardless of the reason'). A second, softer near-synonym is 그래서 그랬구나 'so that's why,' which is more explicit; 어쩐지 keeps it punchy. It works in casual and softly polite speech alike — just surround it with 요-level verbs for politeness. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 'why' (왜): 어쩐지 is not a question, it is a satisfied 'ah, no wonder.'

english: Anyway / by the way — used to change the subject or get back to what matters.
usage: dropping one thread for a new one
leading warmly into the new topic
pivoting straight into a new question
examples: 그나저나 저녁 뭐 먹지?
Anyway, what should we eat for dinner?
the bare pivot to a fresh topic
그래, 그것도 맞아. 그나저나 너 이사 준비는 잘 돼 가?
Yeah, that's true too. By the way, is your moving prep going okay?
everyday: closing one point, then raising what you actually care about
A: 그 얘긴 됐고 / B: 그나저나 주말에 시간 돼?
A: Enough about that / B: Anyway, are you free this weekend?
real situation: deliberately dropping a topic to set up a plan
nuance: 그나저나 means 'anyway / by the way' and its job is to DROP the current thread and bring up something else you actually want to talk about — a topic switch, not a wrap-up. It comes from 그러나저러나 'this way or that way,' so it literally shrugs off the previous talk to pivot. The contrast you must keep sharp is with 아무튼/어쨌든: those CONCLUDE the present topic and drive to its point, whereas 그나저나 abandons it for a NEW one — answer 'so what's the conclusion?' with 그나저나 and you've changed the subject instead of finishing. It feels casual and warm, like a friendly nudge ('oh, by the way…'), and pairs habitually with 말이야 or a follow-up question (그나저나 밥은?). It is fine in everyday polite talk, but in formal writing or business email it is too chatty; there you use 그건 그렇고 or 다름이 아니라. English speakers map all of 'anyway / by the way / regardless' onto one word, so they reach for 그나저나 when they mean to conclude — that is the trap.

Confusing it with 그러나 'however' because they look alike — 그러나 contrasts ideas within one topic, while 그나저나 leaves the topic entirely.

english: Anyway / in any case — used to wrap up or push past a tangent to the main point.
examples: 아무튼 결론은 못 가.
Anyway, the point is I can't go.
the bare wrap-up to a conclusion
설명하자면 길어. 아무튼 도와줘서 진짜 고마워.
It's a long story. Anyway, thanks so much for the help.
everyday: brushing past details to land the real message
A: 그래서 어떻게 됐는데? / B: 아무튼 잘 끝났어.
A: So how did it turn out? / B: Anyway, it ended fine.
real situation: glossing over the messy middle and giving the upshot
nuance: 아무튼 means 'anyway / regardless' and is used to brush past the details and LAND on what counts — it concludes the current thread rather than opening a new one. It is built from 아무 'any' + the -든 'whichever' ending, so it literally says 'whatever the case, here's the point.' Two contrasts matter. First, against 그나저나: 그나저나 switches to a different topic, while 아무튼 wraps up THIS one — they are not interchangeable even though both translate as 'anyway.' Second, against its closest twin 어쨌든: the two are near-identical and usually swappable, but 어쨌든 leans a hair more on 'no matter what the situation,' often after weighing options, while 아무튼 is the everyday 'anyhow, moving on.' It rides from casual to polite comfortably; 아무튼 간에 adds a touch more 'no matter what.' The English-speaker pitfall is using one English 'anyway' to cover both the topic-switch and the wrap-up — in Korean those are 그나저나 and 아무튼, and mixing them confuses listeners.

Stretching 아무튼 to mean 'either way both options are fine' — for genuinely weighing two outcomes, 어쨌든 fits better; 아무튼 just signals 'enough detail, here's the point.'

english: Anyway / either way / regardless — moves on while setting aside whatever was just said.
examples: 어쨌든 됐어.
Either way, it's fine.
the bare 'regardless, that settles it'
이유야 어쨌든, 결국 늦은 건 늦은 거야.
Whatever the reason, late is late in the end.
everyday: acknowledging a reason but dismissing it
A: 환불은 어렵다고 하던데 / B: 어쨌든 한번 문의는 해 봐.
A: They said a refund is hard / B: Either way, try asking once.
real situation: pushing forward in spite of the obstacle
nuance: 어쨌든 means 'either way / regardless' — you acknowledge what was just said, declare it doesn't change the outcome, and move on. It is 어찌하- 'however it be' + 었 + the -든 'whichever' ending, so it literally carries 'however things turned out.' Its near-twin is 아무튼, and in most sentences they swap freely; the fine line is that 어쨌든 leans harder on 'no matter what the situation/reason' — it often follows a reason you are setting aside (이유야 어쨌든) — while 아무튼 is the plainer 'anyhow, here's the point.' Keep it apart, too, from 그나저나, which abandons the topic for a new one rather than concluding it. It works in casual and polite speech alike, and 어쨌거나 is a fully interchangeable variant. Two English-speaker traps: spelling — it is 어쨌든, never 어쨋든 (the middle syllable is 쨌, written with a double ㅆ batchim, not 쩟); and overuse — leaning on 어쨌든 to wave away every objection can sound dismissive, so use it when you genuinely mean 'that aside, let's proceed.'

Treating 어쨌든 and 그나저나 as the same 'anyway' — 어쨌든 concludes/sets aside the current point, while 그나저나 switches to a new topic entirely.

english: That's true, but… — agreeing partly while raising a 'but' or hesitation.
examples: 그렇긴 한데…
That's true, but…
the bare concede-then-hedge, trailing off
A: 거기 싸고 좋잖아 / B: 그렇긴 한데 너무 멀어.
A: It's cheap and nice there / B: True, but it's too far.
everyday: granting the point, then the real objection after -ㄴ데
A: 운동 좀 해야 돼 / B: 그렇긴 해요. 시간이 없어서요.
A: You should work out / B: That's true. It's just I have no time.
real situation: polite half-agreement softening a 'but'
nuance: 그렇긴 한데 means 'that's true, but…' — you grant the other person's point with 그렇긴 (그렇다 'be so' + the contrast-marking -긴), then -ㄴ데 swings the door open for your reservation. The whole move is a gentle, face-saving disagreement: concede first so the 'but' doesn't sting. The contrast to internalize is with a flat 아니 'no' or 그건 아니지 'that's not it': those reject head-on, while 그렇긴 한데 keeps the other person's dignity by agreeing partway first — Korean conversation strongly prefers this cushioned route. Note also that the -긴 here carries a faint 'true ENOUGH, but…' reluctance that plain 그런데 lacks. It is casual; for polite speech say 그렇긴 한데요 or 그렇긴 해요 and continue. The English-speaker pitfalls are two: spacing — 긴 attaches to 그렇 (그렇긴), it is never 그렇 긴; and skipping the concession and jumping straight to the objection, which in Korean lands as blunt and a little cold.

Forgetting to make it polite when needed — to a senior, plain 그렇긴 한데 is banmal; use 그렇긴 한데요 or 그렇긴 해요 and then state your reservation.

english: Of course / absolutely — a warm, emphatic 'yes, definitely' in polite speech.
examples: 그럼요.
Of course.
the bare warm 'absolutely, yes'
A: 자리 좀 맡아 주실 수 있어요? / B: 그럼요, 앉으세요.
A: Could you save my seat? / B: Of course, have a seat.
everyday: agreeing warmly to a small request
A: 이거 정말 가져가도 돼요? / B: 그럼요, 편하게 드세요.
A: Can I really take this? / B: Of course, help yourself.
real situation: reassuring a hesitant guest generously
nuance: 그럼요 is a warm, confident 'of course / absolutely' that reassures the listener you fully agree or gladly say yes — it radiates welcome, not mere consent. It is 그렇다 'to be so' contracted to 그럼 plus the polite -요, so it literally affirms 'it certainly IS so.' Its near-synonym is 당연하죠 'naturally/obviously,' and the two often stack (그럼요, 당연하죠) for extra warmth; the subtle difference is that 당연하죠 stresses 'that goes without saying,' while 그럼요 stresses friendly readiness. The plain-speech version is 그럼 for friends. The crucial English-speaker pitfall is a homograph clash: the SAME letters 그럼 also serve as the transition word 'then / in that case' (그럼 가자 'then let's go'). With the -요 attached, 그럼요 is almost always the emphatic 'of course'; the connective sense is the bare 그럼 plus a clause. Mixing them up makes you answer a yes/no question with 'well then…', which is confusing. Collocations: 그럼요 readily precedes 앉으세요 / 드세요 / 그렇게 하세요 when you grant something.

With the -요 attached, 그럼요 is almost always the emphatic 'of course'; the connective sense is the bare 그럼 plus a clause. Mixing them up makes you answer a yes/no question with 'well then…', which is confusing.

mistakes: Confusing 그럼요 (of course) with the transition 그럼 (then / in that case) — 그럼요 with -요 is an emphatic 'yes, of course,' while bare 그럼 + a clause means 'then…'; answering a question with the connective sense sounds off.
Saying plain 그럼 to a customer, senior, or stranger when you mean 'of course' — that is casual; the polite warm form is 그럼요.
Using 그럼요 to mean a neutral, lukewarm 'yes' — it is emphatic and warm ('absolutely!'); for a flat, factual yes use 네 / 예 instead.

english: Right? / I know / told you — sympathetic agreement, often with a hint of 'yeah, exactly.'
examples: 그러게 말이야.
Right, exactly.
the bare strong 'totally, I feel the same'
A: 날씨 진짜 춥다 / B: 그러게, 갑자기 겨울 됐어.
A: It's so cold / B: I know, it suddenly turned winter.
everyday: warmly echoing a friend's complaint
A: 진작 예약할걸 / B: 그러게, 자리가 없네.
A: We should've booked sooner / B: Right, there are no seats.
real situation: shared regret with a soft 'told you' undertone
nuance: 그러게 is a sympathetic 'right? / I know' that signals you feel EXACTLY the same — most often about something mildly annoying, regrettable, or that you half-predicted, so it can carry a soft 'told you so.' It comes from 그러다 'to be/do so' + the -게 ending and works as a fellow-feeling echo. The contrast to fix is against 그렇구나: 그러게 agrees with a feeling you ALREADY share ('yeah, I know, right?'), while 그렇구나 receives a NEW fact you didn't know ('oh, I see') — answer 'it's freezing' with 그렇구나 and you sound like cold weather is breaking news. A second near-synonym is 내 말이(야) 'that's exactly what I'm saying,' which is even more emphatic and pairs with it (그러게, 내 말이). Use 그러게 with friends, 그러게요 with people you keep -요 with, and 그러게 말이야 to ramp the agreement up. The English-speaker pitfall is mishearing the rising tone as the question 'why did you do that?' — it is purely an agreeing reaction, not a 'why.'

Saying plain 그러게 to a senior — it is banmal; with someone you keep -요 with, use 그러게요.

english: Since you said so / because they were like that — explains why you acted, reacting to what someone said or did.
usage: reacting to their words or actions
examples: 네가 그러길래 그랬지.
I did it because you said so.
the bare 'you prompted me, so I acted'
네가 먹고 싶다 그러길래 사 왔어.
You said you wanted some, so I bought it.
everyday: your action explained by their words
A: 왜 먼저 갔어? / B: 다들 바쁘다 그러길래.
A: Why'd you leave first? / B: Everyone said they were busy, so…
real situation: the reason trails off, the result left implied
nuance: 그러길래 explains YOUR own action as a reaction to what someone ELSE said or did — 'since you/they were like that, I…'. It is 그러다 'to do/be so' + the connective -길래, and the defining feature is that -길래 always points the cause at the other party, never at yourself: that is exactly what separates it from plain 그래서, which is a neutral 'so' that can take any subject. So 비가 와서 우산을 샀어 (it rained, neutral cause) is fine, but to say 'YOU kept saying it's good, so I tried it' you need 하도 맛있다고 그러길래 시켜 봤어 — the cause sits with them. It is casual and conversational, the reason frequently trailing off with the result left implied (다들 바쁘다 그러길래…). A close cousin is -기에, which means the same but is more written/formal; -길래 is the spoken form. The English-speaker pitfall: learners use 그러길래 for their own internal reason (because I was tired, because I wanted to) — for that you must use 그래서, since -길래 demands an external trigger from someone else.

english: I guess so / it seems so — a soft guess based on what you're seeing or hearing.
examples: 그런가 봐요.
I guess so.
the bare soft guess from a hunch
불이 꺼져 있네요. 오늘 쉬는 날인가 봐요.
The lights are off. I guess they're closed today.
everyday: inferring from a visible clue
A: 비 오려나 / B: 하늘 보니까 그런가 봐.
A: Is it going to rain / B: Looking at the sky, I guess so.
real situation: 보니까 + 그런가 봐 grounds the guess in evidence
nuance: 그런가 봐요 means 'I guess so / it seems so' and is used to make a SOFT inference from something you observe rather than to state a fact outright. The engine is the ending -(으)ㄴ가/나 보다 'it looks like / I guess,' which marks a guess drawn from external evidence, so 그런가 봐요 = 'from what I can see, it seems to be so.' The contrast that matters is against -겠- and against 것 같다. -겠다 (그렇겠어요) is a quicker, more confident 'it must be so' from reasoning, while -나 보다 leans on observed evidence and stays more tentative; 그런 것 같아요 is very close but slightly more subjective ('I think so'), whereas 그런가 봐요 implies 'the signs suggest so.' Drop to 그런가 봐 with friends, and flip to 아닌가 봐요 for 'I guess not.' Two English-speaker pitfalls: spacing — standard is 그런가 봐요, with 봐요 written separately as the auxiliary (not 그런가봐요); and don't use -나 보다 about your OWN feelings or actions — you don't 'guess' your own state, so '배고픈가 봐요' about yourself is odd unless you mean it half-jokingly.

Swapping it for confident -겠어요 when you only have a hunch — 그런가 봐요 is tentative (evidence-based guess); 그렇겠어요 sounds like a firmer 'it must be so.'

english: Now that you mention it / hearing you say that — you reconsider after listening to someone.
usage: with -까 leading into a fuller clause
examples: 듣고 보니 그러네.
Now that you say it, yeah.
the bare 'on hearing it, you're right'
A: 이 색이 너한테 더 어울려 / B: 듣고 보니 네 말이 맞는 것 같아.
A: This color suits you better / B: Now that you mention it, I think you're right.
everyday: coming around to their view after listening
듣고 보니까 그 식당 좀 비싸긴 했어.
Come to think of it, that restaurant was kind of pricey.
real situation: recalling and re-judging once the topic comes up
nuance: 듣고 보니 literally stacks 듣다 'to hear' + -고 보니 'having done and then found,' so it means 'now that I've heard it (and looked back), I realize…' — you take in what someone said and reconsider, almost always ending up agreeing. The -고 보니 frame is a 'do X, then discover' construction (cf. 가 보니 'on going, I found,' 자고 보니 'after sleeping, I realized'), which is why it signals a fresh after-the-fact realization rather than a prior opinion. The contrast to keep is against 그러게: 그러게 means 'right, I already felt the same,' but 듣고 보니 means 'I hadn't seen it that way until you said it — and now I do,' so it foregrounds a CHANGE of mind. It naturally flows into 그렇네 or 맞네 to mark that the penny dropped. It is comfortable in casual and polite speech; add -까 (듣고 보니까) before a longer follow-up clause. The English-speaker pitfall is reading -고 보니 as a plain 'after listening' time sequence — in conversation it specifically conveys 'on second thought, I now agree,' not just chronology.
